subject: Cognitive Science
title: Garden Path Sentences
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Garden Path Sentences.

hook.text: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Read it again. It's a real sentence—but your brain got tricked.

buildup.text: A garden path sentence leads you down one interpretation, then forces you to backtrack and reparse.

discovery.text: Your brain commits to a structure immediately, word by word. It doesn't wait for the full sentence.

twist.text: Eye-tracking shows readers physically regress—their eyes jump backward—exactly at the point of confusion.

climax.text: This proves that parsing is incremental and greedy. The brain takes the simplest structure and only revises when forced.

punchline.text: Your brain bets on meaning before the sentence ends.

quiz.question: What does a garden path sentence reveal about parsing?
options: The brain commits to structure immediately
We wait for the whole sentence first

details.summary: Garden path sentences lead readers to an initial interpretation that turns out wrong. The horse raced past the barn fell makes you reparse because raced was initially read as past tense but is actually a reduced relative clause.
details.whyItMatters: Garden path sentences are a window into real-time sentence processing. They show that the brain commits to one interpretation immediately rather than waiting for complete information.
takeaways: Readers commit to one parse before the sentence is complete
Garden path sentences force costly reanalysis mid-sentence
They reveal the incremental nature of language processing

faq.question: Why does the brain commit to one parse so early?
faq.answer: Speed. Language arrives at three to four words per second, and waiting for complete information would overwhelm working memory. The parser uses frequency-based heuristics, defaulting to the most common structure.

faq.question: What happens in the brain during a garden path?
faq.answer: EEG studies show a distinctive P600 brainwave when readers encounter the disambiguating word, reflecting the cost of reanalysis. Reading time increases dramatically at the point of disambiguation. Eye-tracking shows regressions back to earlier parts of the sentence as the reader attempts to reparse.
